title: Check your understanding: Searching Repository History

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the purpose of searching repository history?
options: History searches filter commits by message, author, date or changes to content. Search results are limited by the references and paths examined, so missing a result does not prove the change never existed in another clone or ref.
Git automatically backs up every file, including ignored and untracked files, to a remote.
The operation grants every contributor write access to the hosted repository.
questions.answer_key: History searches filter commits by message, author, date or changes to content. Search results are limited by the references and paths examined, so missing a result does not prove the change never existed in another clone or ref.
questions.explanation: History searches filter commits by message, author, date or changes to content. Search results are limited by the references and paths examined, so missing a result does not prove the change never existed in another clone or ref.

questions.prompt: Which command is the most direct starting point for this lesson’s example?
questions.explanation: Use `git log --all --grep="fix" --oneline` as the first inspection/action in the example, and then verify the result with the companion checks in the lesson.

questions.prompt: Which is the safest general practice when working with searching repository history?
options: Inspect the repository state, verify the expected result, and protect valuable work before destructive or history-changing operations.
Run the most destructive option first; the reflog guarantees every file can always be recovered.
Assume the local command also changed the remote and satisfied all hosting-platform policies.
questions.answer_key: Inspect the repository state, verify the expected result, and protect valuable work before destructive or history-changing operations.
questions.explanation: Inspect the repository state, verify the expected result, and protect valuable work before destructive or history-changing operations.
